blocks.title: Introduction
blocks.content:
When a research library acquires a book, a profes-
sional cataloger reads it and attaches a small set
of standardised labels describing what it is about.
For English-language cataloging worldwide these la-
bels are drawn from the Library of Congress Subject
Headings (LCSH) (Library of Congress, n.d.), a con-
trolled vocabulary of roughly half a million autho-
rised headings, many further refined by subdivisions
(e.g. Sociology--Research). Subject access of this kind
is what lets a reader find everything a collection holds
on a topic, independent of the words an author chose.
Assigning it well

summary.text: Introduction and contributions. LCSH is a controlled vocabulary of roughly half a million authorised headings, many refined by subdivisions, and assigning it is slow expert work that software and LLMs may assist; but unlike GND (LLMs4Subjects), MeSH (BioASQ) or EuroVoc (MultiEURLEX), LCSH has no standard public benchmark, so published numbers cannot be compared. LCSHBench v1.0 contributes a consensus-grounded dataset of 22,346 books in 15 languages, admitted when at least two independent cataloging agencies assigned LCSH, with a default union answer key (about 46% of development assertions are single-source) plus unanimous and per-catalog views, and further contributions on concordance, tasks, metrics and baselines.

blocks.title: Front matter
blocks.content:
LCSHBench: A Multilingual, Consensus-Grounded Benchmark for
Library of Congress Subject Heading Assignment
Kwok Leong Tang
2026-06-01
Abstract
Automated subject cataloging assigns controlled-
vocabulary headings to bibliographic records, but
LCSH has no standard public benchmark. We intro-
duce LCSHBench: 22,346 books in 15 languages from
the openly licensed Harvard, Columbia, and Prince-
ton catalogs. Records enter only when at least two
independent cataloging agencies assigned LCSH; we
release per-catalog provenance plus union and unani-
mous answer views. A concordance study of 465,187
work

summary.text: Title, author and abstract of "LCSHBench: A Multilingual, Consensus-Grounded Benchmark for Library of Congress Subject Heading Assignment" by Kwok Leong Tang (2026-06-01). The paper introduces a public, versioned benchmark for automated assignment of Library of Congress Subject Headings, built from books that independent professional catalogers in several research libraries cataloged, and scores systems with a panel of metrics rather than one headline number.

blocks.title: Literature review
blocks.content:
This work sits at the intersection of three literatures:
the cataloging-theory tradition on what a “subject”
is and how reliably it can be assigned; the automated
subject-indexing literature on systems that assign it;
and the benchmark literature in adjacent controlled
vocabularies. We draw on all three, and locate the
gap each leaves for LCSH.
2.1
What a “subject” is: subject anal-
ysis and aboutness
Subject cataloging begins with subject analysis —
determining what a work is about and rendering
that judgement as controlled-vocabulary headings
(Joudrey and Taylor 2018). Hjørland’s foundationa

summary.text: Literature review, part one. The work draws on cataloging theory, automated subject indexing and benchmarks in adjacent vocabularies. On what a subject is, Hjørland argues that a subject is a judgement shaped by the analyst's purpose rather than a property read off a document, so there is no single gold answer and a key must come from agreement among experts, which the consensus design operationalises. On inter-indexer consistency, studies since Zunde and Dexter (1969) and Leonard's review (1977) find that independent indexers agree on exact terms only modestly, commonly in the 10–50% range, with consistency rising as terms are generalised.

blocks.title: Automated subject indexing
blocks.content:
Automated subject indexing has a long applied his-
tory, surveyed comprehensively by Golub (Golub
2021). The dominant open toolkit is Annif (Suomi-
nen 2019), which combines string-matching and su-
pervised extreme-multi-label learning and underpins
production services at several national libraries; re-
cent work adapts transformer-based extreme-multi-
label classifiers to subject indexing (Bertalis et al.
2024). These systems are typically trained and evalu-
ated against a single institution’s headings, which —
given the consistency results above — conflates gen-
uine error with legitimate ca

summary.text: Literature review, part two. Automated subject indexing is surveyed by Golub; the main open toolkit, Annif, combines string matching with extreme multi-label learning, but such systems are usually trained and evaluated against one institution's headings, conflating error with legitimate cataloger variation. On LLMs, Chow, Kao and Li used ChatGPT to generate LCSH for theses and concluded that human catalogers remain essential; the German National Library's DNB-AI ranked fourth by F1 but first by expert rating in SemEval-2025, which the author calls the most important prior result because numeric and expert rankings diverge; Chow's agentic pipeline and hybrid embedding-plus-LLM pipelines are also noted.
A section number only: the start of the Methodology (3.1).

blocks.title: The two tasks
blocks.content:
A system takes a book’s bibliographic fields and pro-
poses subject headings. We score two tasks that iso-
late different abilities.
Task A — Generation (open vocabulary). Given only
3
the bibliographic fields, the system must produce the
correct headings from the entire vocabulary, with no
hints. This is the realistic, end-to-end task a human
cataloger performs. Output is an unordered set of
headings.
Task B — Retrieval pipeline (retrieve →rerank →se-
lect). Many practical systems work in stages: a fast
first stage retrieves a rough shortlist from the vocabu-
lary, and later stages re-examine

summary.text: The two tasks. A system takes a book's bibliographic fields and proposes subject headings. Task A is open-vocabulary generation: from the fields alone, produce an unordered set of headings from the whole vocabulary, as a cataloger does. Task B is a staged pipeline over the full released vocabulary of about 515,000 LCSH and LCGFT labels: retrieval of the top k headings (L1, whose recall bounds everything downstream), cross-encoder reranking (L2), LLM reranking (L3) and selection of the final set (L4, scored like Task A). This replaces a frozen per-record candidate pool, which would bake in one retriever's choices and hide the embedding model, the component most worth measuring.

blocks.title: Consensus ground truth
blocks.content:
There is no single correct heading set for a book —
cataloging is expert judgement, and while profession-
als largely agree on a work’s subject they vary in how
they express it, as shown in Section 3.3. We therefore
define ground truth by consensus across independent
libraries: the same book is cataloged separately by
several research libraries, and where independent ex-
perts agree we have something close to truth. The
inclusion rule is strict and never relaxed to enlarge
the dataset: a book is admitted only if at least two
libraries independently assigned LCSH to it.
Inde-
pendence is enforc

summary.text: Consensus ground truth and inter-cataloger concordance. Since cataloging is expert judgement, ground truth is defined by agreement across independent libraries: a book is admitted only if at least two libraries independently assigned LCSH, with independence enforced at the cataloging agency (MARC 040) so copy-cataloged records do not count twice, and the rule is never relaxed to enlarge the dataset. To test whether experts agree enough, the paper compares the 465,187 works subject-cataloged by all three libraries, using three-way and mean-pairwise Jaccard indices under exact and concept matching (Table 1): 93.3% share a concept-level heading but only 39.4% have identical heading sets, 35.6% of assertions are single-source, and median three-way Jaccard is 0.50 exact and 0.86 concept. A human cataloger reproduces about 87% (exact) and 93% (concept) of peers' consensus.

blocks.title: Sources and matching
blocks.content:
The raw material is openly licensed bulk MARC from
research libraries — Harvard, Columbia, and Prince-
ton (the Library of Congress dump was considered
but dropped, as its coverage stops at 2014). All are
CC0 / public domain, so the benchmark redistributes
the actual records, making it fully reproducible. The
same book is identified across catalogs by OCLC
number (primary) and LCCN (fallback); a subtle
but high-impact step strips the historical ocm/ocn/on
prefixes and leading zeros from OCLC numbers and
rejects all-zero identifiers, without which matching
silently fails — or, worse, collapses

summary.text: Sources, matching and extraction. The data are CC0 bulk MARC from Harvard, Columbia and Princeton (the Library of Congress dump was dropped because coverage stops in 2014), so actual records are redistributed. Books are matched by OCLC number, with LCCN as fallback, after stripping ocm/ocn/on prefixes and leading zeros and rejecting all-zero identifiers, without which matching fails or merges unrelated records. Inputs are title, authors, date, publisher, physical description, summary, contents and notes, with language and broad discipline; answers are the 6xx headings reassembled with subdivisions. Provenance filtering keeps 600–651 headings only with second indicator 0 or $2 lcsh, and 655 only with $2 lcgft, removing many FAST, MeSH and foreign-vocabulary strings that look like LCSH; headings are then typed by MARC field (topical 65.9%, geographic 17.4%, name 14.3%, genre/form 2.2%), and 78.8% carry subdivisions.

blocks.content:

tion 1) is tiered unanimous if 𝑣= 𝑛, single if
𝑣= 1, and majority otherwise; from which we re-
lease three answer-key views: per-catalog (the raw
evidence), merged/union (the default; rewards find-

(the strictest, highest-confidence view).
Headings
are cleaned by discarding MARC-machinery artifacts
(strings whose base matches a ^\d{3}[-/] field-tag
pattern) and by canonical normalization before any
comparison: NFC, lower-casing, -- separator ca

summary.text: Consensus views and cleaning. A heading asserted by v of the n libraries holding a book is tiered unanimous if v = n, single if v = 1 and majority otherwise, and three answer-key views are released: per-catalog (the raw evidence), merged union (the default, rewarding any heading a professional used) and unanimous (the strictest). Headings are cleaned by discarding MARC field-tag artifacts and normalised before comparison (NFC, lower-casing, canonical -- separators, collapsed whitespace, trailing periods stripped), so systems are judged on substance rather than typography.

blocks.title: Balancing and splits
blocks.content:
Naively harvested cross-library matches are badly
skewed:
heavily co-collected, uniformly identified
Western art music floods the pool, and a few Euro-
pean languages crowd out the rest. We correct this
at selection by stratified sampling over LC classifica-
tion (round-robin across disciplines with a hard 5%
music cap) and language (explicit per-language tar-
gets and floors). All randomness is driven by a fixed
seed, so builds are reproducible. To avoid letting in-
put scarcity distort which books appear, we select
first and enrich second: books are chosen on consen-
sus, discipline, and lan

summary.text: Balancing and splits. Naively harvested cross-library matches are skewed toward heavily co-collected Western art music and a few European languages, so selection uses stratified sampling over LC classification (round-robin across disciplines with a hard 5% music cap) and over language (per-language targets and floors), driven by a fixed seed. Books are chosen on consensus, discipline and language alone, and only then is each one's input completed with the longest non-empty value of each field across its libraries. The collection is split, balanced by language, into a public development set and a held-out test set.

blocks.title: Composition
blocks.content:
LCSHBench v1.0 contains 22,346 books (develop-
ment 18,993; test 3,353), none discarded for empty
answers. It spans 15 languages, with English delib-
erately held to 23.2% (German and French 10.1%
each; Chinese, Spanish, and Russian 8.1%;
Ital-
ian, Arabic, and Japanese 6.4%; Korean and Por-
tuguese 5.0%; down to Hindi 0.1%). Across the LC-
classification areas present the collection is near-flat
(~3.2–5.0% each), with music pinned at its 5.0% cap
and ~4.8% of books carrying no classification. 66.1%
of books rest on two-library agreement and 33.9%
on three. Roughly a quarter carry an original-

summary.text: Composition. LCSHBench v1.0 contains 22,346 books (development 18,993, test 3,353), none discarded for empty answers, across 15 languages with English deliberately held to 23.2%; 66.1% of books rest on two-library agreement and 33.9% on three.

blocks.title: Contamination
blocks.content:
The test answers are released only as SHA-256 hashes
of normalized headings, so scoring is exact and auto-
matic without the answers appearing verbatim. In
the public release, record identifiers (OCLC, LCCN)
are likewise replaced by an opaque hashed key — pre-
serving each work’s stable identity for linking and
scoring without redistributing the source libraries’
identifier numbers in bulk. (The construction repos-
itory retains raw identifiers as a build artifact; the
distinction is between the internal build and the pub-
lished dataset.) We are explicit that the test-answer
hashing is a spee

summary.text: Contamination. Test answers are released only as SHA-256 hashes of normalised headings, so scoring is exact and automatic without the answers appearing verbatim; the author treats this as a speed-bump, not a guarantee, since hashes over a finite public vocabulary can be dictionary-attacked.

blocks.title: Metrics
blocks.content:
The central methodological commitment is that no
single number is trustworthy on its own: an aggre-
gate can hide catastrophic per-language or per-type
failure, and can rank systems against the grain of
expert judgement (Galke et al. 2022; D’Souza et al.
2025). We report a panel and read the pattern across
it.
For generation, predictions and answers are sets; we
report micro- and macro-averaged precision, recall,
and F1.
For the retrieval pipeline, predictions are
ranked and we report recall@𝑘(𝑘∈{5, 10, 50, 200}),
P@𝑘, R-Precision, and MRR. Every measure is com-
puted under two match defini

summary.text: Metrics. No single number is trusted on its own, because an aggregate can hide per-language or per-type failure and can rank systems against expert judgement. Generation is scored as sets with micro- and macro-averaged precision, recall and F1; the retrieval pipeline with recall@k (k = 5, 10, 50, 200), P@k, R-precision and MRR. Every measure is computed under exact matching (the full subdivided heading) and concept matching (the base term before the first --); a high concept but low exact score means the right topic in the wrong authorised form. Every measure is also broken down by language and heading type, which the paper calls the panel's most important safeguard. Retrieval is scored against the gold headings reachable in the vocabulary, with the ceiling reported (41% of gold headings exact, 85% concept, on the evaluation subset; name headings are reported separately) and only records with at least one reachable heading averaged: 1,483 of 2,002 for exact, 1,929 for concept, with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals.

— a trivial, input-independent baseline that ex-

• Stock on-device embedder. EmbeddingGemma-
300M embeddings over the full vocabulary at the

local retriever, untouched.
• Hosted
embedders.
OpenAI
text-emb

summary.text: Baselines and setup. Reference systems run on the development set, the neural ones on a deterministic, language-stratified 2,002-record subset (the full run is deferred for cost): a frequency floor predicting the 200 most frequent development headings for every record; stock EmbeddingGemma-300M at 256 dimensions; OpenAI text-embedding-3-small (1,536 dimensions) and -large (3,072); and the same EmbeddingGemma backbone with a low-rank fine-tune, the only system trained on the benchmark's records, under a strict leakage protocol.

blocks.title: Fine-tuning the on-device embedder
blocks.content:
The L1 results below show the stock on-device embed-
der trailing the hosted APIs, and the per-language
panel localizes why: the gap is largest where a multi-
lingual record must be matched to an English head-
ing. We treat that as a hypothesis — that the bottle-
neck is cross-lingual alignment, not model capacity —
and address it directly by fine-tuning the 300M model
to map a record to its English headings.
The recipe is cheap and fully reproducible.
We
build (record, heading) training pairs by taking, for
each development record outside the evaluation sub-
set, its merged-consensus LCSH hea

summary.text: Fine-tuning the on-device embedder. Because the stock model trails most where multilingual records must match English headings, the author hypothesises that the bottleneck is cross-lingual alignment, not capacity, and fine-tunes it on (record, heading) pairs from development records outside the evaluation subset: a rank-16 LoRA adapter, multiple-negatives ranking loss inside a Matryoshka loss over 768/512/256/128 dimensions, one epoch on one commodity GPU (about fifteen minutes, under one US dollar), merged and exported to the same on-device runtime. Leakage control excludes evaluation records by identifier and by a title–first-author key, and an audit finds residual overlap at the held-out test's incidental collision rate.
A section number only: the start of the Findings (4.1).

summary.text: First-stage retrieval, generation and selection (Table 2). Off the shelf, the hosted embedders beat the stock on-device model at every depth, larger before smaller. After fine-tuning, on this development subset, the 300M on-device model reaches exact recall@200 of 0.659 against 0.623 for text-embedding-3-large and 0.511 for -small, a small lead the paper reports as significant (paired approximate-randomisation test, +0.036, p = 0.0004) and as pending held-out-test confirmation; against its own stock backbone it rises from 0.407 (+62%). The frequency floor scores 0.130. In Task A the LLM gets the best set scores: generation F1 0.161 exact and 0.384 concept, selection 0.118 and 0.318.

summary.text: Why the metric panel is needed. The aggregate lead does not mean "the on-device model wins". By metric, the fine-tune leads on exact recall@200 (0.659 vs 0.623) but text-embedding-3-large leads on concept recall@200 (0.762 vs 0.732, p = 0.0001), the same exact-versus-concept axis on which catalogers disagree. By language (Table 3), the fine-tune wins Korean (0.668 vs 0.517), Arabic (0.689 vs 0.540), Japanese (0.593 vs 0.537), Chinese (0.618 vs 0.600) and German (0.704 vs 0.651), but the hosted model still leads on English (0.710 vs 0.696) and Russian (0.543 vs 0.505), so the win comes from closing the cross-lingual gap.

blocks.title: Discussion
blocks.content:
Cataloging is reproducible about topic,
variable
about expression — and that shapes everything. The
concordance analysis in Section 3.3 reframes the folk
view that subject assignment is “subjective.”
It is,
but at a specific layer: three independent libraries
converge on what a book is about (concept agree-
ment 93.3%) while differing on how to say it (exact-
identical 39.4%). This is why a single library’s head-
ings make a noisy gold standard, why a consensus
target is worth the construction cost, and why exact
match alone is the wrong yardstick — it penalizes a
model for a subdivision choic

summary.text: Discussion. Cataloging is reproducible about topic and variable about expression: libraries agree on concept (93.3%) but rarely on exact sets (39.4%), so a single library's headings make a noisy gold standard and exact match alone penalises choices catalogers themselves make differently. Human agreement (about 87% exact, 93% concept) is a reference, not a ceiling for recall@200, because a retriever gets 200 candidates while a cataloger gives a short set. A 256-dimensional, 300M-parameter embedder with no network or per-query cost out-retrieves a hosted API on exact recall after a sub-dollar fine-tune, which matters for libraries with privacy, cost or connectivity constraints, though the hosted model remains preferable for mainly English collections.

blocks.title: Limitations and future work
blocks.content:
Consensus is record-level, not heading-level. A book
qualifies on agency-independent agreement, but the
default merged key still includes single-source head-
ings; we release the unanimous view for studies that
need heading-level agreement, and report which view
a result uses.
The neural leaderboard is on a 2K subset. The small-
est languages (Hindi, with a handful of evaluation
records, Turkish, Hebrew) are individually noisy and
should be read as indicative; the held-out test set
(3,353 records) is the basis for the eventual full-scale
evaluation. Scaling the neural runs to full develop-
men

summary.text: Limitations and future work. Consensus is record-level, not heading-level, so the default key includes single-source headings. Neural results are on a 2K development subset, with the smallest languages (Hindi, Turkish, Hebrew) noisy. The fine-tune result is preliminary: development subset only, first stage only, not run through reranking and selection, and not confirmed on the held-out test, though an earlier overlapping variant inflated recall@200 by only about 0.03; the benchmark does not depend on it. Hashed answers are a convenience, not a guarantee, and a private evaluation server is future work; the vocabulary is a mid-2026 snapshot.

blocks.title: Conclusion
blocks.content:
LCSHBench provides the missing standard exam for
an important, hitherto unmeasurable task: multilin-
gual subject-heading assignment against the Library
of Congress vocabulary. Its design choices — inde-
pendent multi-catalog consensus, full-vocabulary re-
trieval rather than a frozen pool, provenance-filtered
ground truth, and a metric panel in place of a head-
line F1 — are grounded rather than incidental: the
concordance analysis shows why a consensus tar-
get and concept-level metrics are needed, and every
leaderboard result has a per-cell counter-reading that
a single aggregate would hide

summary.text: Conclusion. LCSHBench is offered as a standard exam for multilingual LCSH assignment, built on independent multi-catalog consensus, full-vocabulary retrieval, provenance-filtered ground truth and a metric panel. Its per-language panel located cross-lingual alignment as the first-stage bottleneck, and the fine-tune that addressed it is reported as a development-subset demonstration, with held-out-test and end-to-end confirmation left as future work. Data, scorer, baselines, fine-tune recipe, leakage audit and seeds are released together.

anonymized in the public release; all randomness is
seed-driven, so reported results

summary.text: Data and code availability: the dataset (development and held-out test splits, the language-balanced evaluation subset, the concordance population and the retrieval vocabulary) is on Hugging Face as kltng/lcshbench, and the scorer, baselines, fine-tuning recipe, leakage audit and release pipeline are on GitHub at kltng/lcshbench. Test answers are released only as hashes, record identifiers are anonymised, and all randomness is seeded so results reproduce exactly.

summary.text: Use of generative AI, followed by the start of the reference list. The author used Anthropic's Claude via Claude Code to help with software for the extraction, scoring and analysis pipeline, with organising and cross-checking the literature, and with drafting, language and typesetting; the data and all reported results were produced by the author through the described pipeline, not generated by AI, and the author reviewed all content and takes full responsibility. The references begin with work on extreme multi-label classification, MultiEURLEX, FAST and agentic LCSH indexing.
